critics.title: The odd couple
critics.quote: My own view is that Hitchcock hoped Herrmann could deliver the goods, but had also come to resent his dependence on him. Hitchcock's insecurity surfaced in Torn Curtain because Herrmann implied that he knew best.
critics.why: Reads the 1966 break as wounded pride: Hitchcock had come to depend on Herrmann and resented a composer who acted as if he knew better.

critics.title: The sound of suspense: Hitchcock and Herrmann [playlist]
critics.quote: Hitchcock tailored the movie’s edit and its sound design to accommodate the music, most famously in Vertigo’s emotional climax. As Robert Burks’s camera glides 360 degrees around Scottie Ferguson (Stewart) and Judy Barton (Kim Novak), there is no dialogue—only Herrmann’s passionate “Scene d’amour.” As Hitchcock told his composer, “We’ll just have the camera and you.”
critics.why: A specific moment where the director built the scene around the music instead of the other way round, so the two were working as equals.

critics.title: 'Hitchcock's Music' by Jack Sullivan
critics.quote: After the final break between the two testy geniuses, Hitchcock worked with Maurice Jarre (Topaz) and John Williams (Family Plot), but perhaps like Scottie in Vertigo, forever searching for a woman to make over into Madeleine, Hitchcock really wanted another Herrmann. And Herrmann, in turn, in his scores for Brian DePalma's Vertigo pastiche Obsession and for Scorsese's Taxi Driver, wanted another director as driven and creative as Hitchcock.
critics.why: After the split each man spent the rest of his career looking for a replacement for the other, framed through Vertigo's own makeover story.

critics.critic: K. J. Donnelly and Steven Rawle
critics.title: Introduction
critics.quote: Alfred Hitchcock was famed for his cameo appearances in his own films, yet in the remake of The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956) Hitchcock also encouraged Herrmann to make a cameo appearance. His appearance at the Albert Hall, conducting the London Symphony Orchestra, marked a rare moment when Hitchcock allowed a collaborator to ‘do as he did’ – almost an admittance of equal status, one might speculate.
critics.why: Herrmann's on-screen cameo conducting at the Albert Hall as the one time Hitchcock let a collaborator share his trademark, close to admitting they were equals.

critics.title: The odd couple
critics.quote: Hitchcock was particularly cross that Herrmann had written music for a farmhouse murder scene when he had told him not to. (Originally Hitchcock had not wanted music for the shower murder in Psycho but had to concede that it worked better with it. He did not want to be proved wrong twice.)
critics.why: Ties the Torn Curtain fight to the Psycho shower scene: Herrmann had overruled him once and been proved right, and Hitchcock would not let it happen a second time.

critics.title: The sound of suspense: Hitchcock and Herrmann [playlist]
critics.quote: If not for Herrmann, Psycho might survive today only in massively shortened form. After viewing a rough cut without music, Hitchcock decided that he had failed in his biggest gamble: a self-financed, low-budget shocker, targeted at young moviegoers hungry for edgy content. Hitch mused about cutting it down and putting it on his TV series. Herrmann watched the cut and saw what the director didn’t.
critics.why: Herrmann's score rescued Psycho after Hitchcock had lost faith in it: the composer saw what the director couldn't.

critics.title: Herrmann & Hitchcock: Symphony of Suspense
critics.quote: Though Hitchcock originally didn’t want music in “Psycho” (and later realized his error in judgment), he was correct in removing any trace of score in his follow-up horror spectacle, thus accentuating the alienation felt by its human characters facing an apocalyptic catastrophe. Yet the fingerprints of Herrmann, who served as a sound consultant and uncredited sound designer, are still felt in every scene.
critics.why: In The Birds, the film without a score, Herrmann still shaped it as sound consultant, so the partnership went beyond writing music.

notes: I re-fetched every readable first-pass piece as raw HTML/PDF with curl and checked each quote against that text. Prospect (Sinyard): I replaced the one-sentence pull with the full two-sentence thesis (resentment of his dependence on Herrmann, Herrmann implying he "knew best") and added a second Sinyard passage: the farmhouse-murder cue in Torn Curtain read against the Psycho shower reversal ("He did not want to be proved wrong twice"). That passage is in parentheses in the original and the quote keeps them verbatim. Partners in Suspense introduction: I dropped the empty "notable pairing of two great authorial figures" line and used the passage on Herrmann's Albert Hall cameo in The Man Who Knew Too Much, which the editors read as "almost an admittance of equal status". The PDF wraps lines and splits that passage across a page break (pp. 2–3); the text is unchanged otherwise. Indie Outlook: I replaced the closing hype line with the passage on The Birds (no score, but Herrmann as sound consultant). The byline is credited to Matt Fagerholm from the page's schema.org Person data (givenName Matt, familyName Fagerholm, author slug mattmovieman), although the visible page shows only "Indie Outlook". Moved to reading: Qobuz (Magenham), whose only candidate is a "rumoured" claim about Psycho that also wrongly counts the later collaborations (it leaves out Torn Curtain); FMR (Hall), whose own prose is summary or praise and whose strong lines are block quotes from Smith's book, not Hall's words; and Kirkus, which is plot summary built on quotations from Smith. Literary Review (Glancy) is paywalled after the first paragraph, and the visible part is about Hitchcock's collaborators in general, so it stays in reading as paywalled. The OUP monograph and Rawle's chapter stay in reading as paywalled. NEW (2): Steven C. Smith's OUPblog essay "The sound of suspense" (2025-10-14, byline "By Steven C. Smith" on the page), which gives two quotes: the Vertigo "We'll just have the camera and you" moment and Psycho being rescued from a cut-down TV fate. Also Michael S. Gant's Metro Silicon Valley review of Jack Sullivan's Hitchcock's Music (issue of 31 Jan–6 Feb 2007), with the Vertigo-makeover reading of the aftermath: each man wanted another of the other. Its two sentences run to about 67 words, slightly over the target.
